extracted.intended_audience: readers of the Philosophical Transactions / natural philosophers, experimentalists, agriculturists and gentleman scientists (17th century)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting prescriptive and evaluative criteria embedded in a 17th‑century natural philosophy journal page: agricultural guidance on sands, experimental hypotheses and procedures about fish bladders, instrument design/calibration for specific gravity tests, and practical notes on poisonous fish and medical/mathematical standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shelliness as indicator of sand quality
rubrics_metrics.description: "if the matter be shelfy, that is the grating of stones, it is of small value. But if it be shelly, then it is good."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shelly sand (broken shells, coralline) is judged superior for use. The text explains types and sources of shell fragments (muscles, oyster-shells, cockles, scollops) and notes coralline and most shelly kinds are best.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sand colour ranking
rubrics_metrics.description: "Of all these sands, the best are accounted, as to colour, first the reddish, next the blue, then the white."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Colour is used as a proxy for composition and value (reddish indicating certain origins, bluish from broken muscles/oysters, white from moor-stones/free-stone and white shells). Colour therefore informs selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sand grain size suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is said that the small is best for the tenant, who only takes to tillage for four years, because it works sooner, and yields a speedy return. The larger grained is said to be better for the landlord and the land; because it lasts longer in the ground, and makes the pasture afterwards the better."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose grain size based on tenure/time-horizon: fine sand gives faster returns but is shorter-lived; coarse sand endures and benefits long-term pasture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preferred sand source and kinds (dredged / sub‑saltwater vs blown)
rubrics_metrics.description: "that which is taken up from under the salt-water, either by dredges, or being left open by the ebbing of the tide. The blown sand is accounted of no use."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sand collected from under seawater (dredged or newly exposed by ebb) is preferred; wind-blown sand is of little value. Coralline and most shelly kinds are highlighted as best.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of drainage/drying on sand quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally, if sand be well drained of the salt-water, so that it may be more conveniently carried, it is better than that which has lain long drying in the sun and wind, which takes off much of its virtue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sand should be drained of salt-water for transport/use; over-dried sand (long in sun/wind) loses beneficial properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of sand application and crop rotation
rubrics_metrics.description: "it is spread on the ground intended for wheat, or usually in the first crop of four, whatever be the grain. For after four crops, it is the custom to leave the land to pasture for 6 or 7 years, before tilling it again."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply sand at the start of a four-crop sequence (often the first crop) and then follow a multi-year pasture fallow (6–7 years) before re‑tillage; mowing of gratten occurs in the first year after tillage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended quantity of sand per Cornish acre by distance
rubrics_metrics.description: "Near the sand, 300 sacks are laid; at other distances 200, or 150, or even 80. And so proportionably in greater distance, even to 20 or 30 sacks in an acre, rather than none."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantities are scaled to transport distance from the source; suggested numeric guidance given (300, 200, 150, 80, down to 20–30 sacks per Cornish acre).

rubrics_metrics.name: Agricultural outcomes as evaluation metrics of sand use
rubrics_metrics.description: "where much sand is used, the seed is much, and the straw little... But where less sand is used, there is much straw, and but little, and that hungry grain."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use observed crop characteristics (seed vs straw proportion, ear length relative to stalk) and post-harvest pasture/grass quality (white clover dominance, early harvest, better garden herbs and fruits, less snow retention) as measures of sand application success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best sand kinds (shelly and coralline) and method of retrieval
rubrics_metrics.description: "As to kinds, the most shelly and the coralline are best: and that which is taken up from under the salt-water..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer shelly/coralline sands taken from under the sea; these are identified as most valuable for husbandry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule de insidentibus humido (buoyancy principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The rule de insidentibus humido, is, that a body that is heavier than so much water as, is equal in quantity to the bulk of it, will sink; a body that is lighter will swim; a body of equal weight will rest in any part of the water."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this hydrostatic principle as a working rule to reason about floating/sinking bodies and to interpret experiments (e.g., fish buoyancy and specific-gravity measurements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fish bladder buoyancy hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: "the air in that bladder is like the bubble, more or less compressed, according to the depth the fish swims at, and takes up more or less space; and consequently the body of the fish... is greater or less according to the several depths, and yet retains the same weight."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hypothesis: fish regulate depth by varying bladder volume (compression with depth); possible mechanisms include emitting or taking in air and muscular contraction of the bladder; this guides experiment design and interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment to test fish bladder action (Boyle's suggested experiment)
rubrics_metrics.description: "take a bolthead with a wide neck, and having filled it almost full with water, to put into it some live fish... then to draw out the neck of the bolthead as slender as you can, and to fill that also almost with water: whereupon the fish... if upon his sinking you perceive the water at the slender top subsides, you may infer that he contracts himself, and if, upon his rising, the water be also raised, you may conclude that he dilates himself."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure and direct inference rules are provided: observe changes in water level in a slender neck to infer contraction/dilation of the fish's volume; use appropriate fish species and vessel geometry to make observations notable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevention and antidotes for fish poisoning
rubrics_metrics.description: "In voyages to remote parts ... the crews ... may often prevent the mischievous consequences arising from the use of the fishes of those seas ... by gutting them immediately after they are taken, and washing them well in clear water (either salt or fresh) before they are dressed."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preventive practice: gut and thoroughly wash suspect tropical fish immediately after capture. Antidotes mentioned for symptoms include Cayenne pepper, Madeira, and other powerful cordials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design specifications for a floating specific-gravity instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: "This instrument ... consists of three parts; viz. the ball, the stem, and that which holds the coin. The ball ... should contain as much air as may serve to keep the whole instrument, when loaded, from sinking beneath the top of the stem. The stem ... should be made very slender ... and ... not be too short..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed construction guidance: ball formed of two thin concave plates with holes for stem and screw; stem slender to accentuate depression changes; removable lower stem/screw and ballast plates for adjustment; use of soldering and fittings described for stability and function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Calibration and testing protocol for coin examination with the floating instrument
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed procedure: hang a known genuine coin, stop the stem orifice, immerse and let settle; adjust ballast so instrument keeps desired posture; mark waterline (H) with genuine coin, replace with brass plate of equal weight and mark (I). To test suspected coin weigh in air and in water and subtract the latter from the former.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calibration uses a genuine reference coin and waterline marks to detect coins that are too light in water (indicating lower fineness) versus coins washed (light in air). The protocol includes how to add/remove ballast and resolve doubts with a balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for mathematical editions (clarity and demonstration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Barrow's edition "delivered these three books in a brief symbolical method of expression, pursuant to the sense, propositions and demonstrations of the ancients; unless where he thought fit to enlarge, and otherwise to demonstrate some of the propositions from more easy principles of his own"; contrasted with fault found in the "obscurity of Rivalt's edition."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial standard: mathematical texts should be clear (avoid obscurity), follow the sense of original propositions, and where helpful provide enlarged or simpler demonstrations to aid understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for medical practice and critique of Paracelsian method
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism: Paracelsus 'pronounced anatomy useless; neglected to investigate the symptoms and progress of diseases; and, instead of searching into their real nature and origin, assigned for their production certain fictitious chemical agents.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit standard for medicine: practitioners should investigate symptoms and disease progression, ground treatment in anatomical and observational knowledge, avoid unintelligible jargon and unsupported magical claims; empirical evidence and careful observation are valued.
